# Continuation from the three dimensional radial Laplacian

27 October 2026, America/New_York. Prepared for **Edward Baker** with substantial LLM assistance, **gpt-6-astra (Codex), actual recorded effort max**. Research conversation **Continue higher-dimensional H-rep**, Investigation05 chat0003, thread 01a17f2b-8196-7683-ab85-434b4bd2ac20.

**Current direction.** Keep the original one-dimensional theta sum and develop its three-dimensional radial interpretation. The useful simplification is that the polynomial weights in Phi are generated by the ordinary radial Laplacian. A three-dimensional discrete lattice is no longer a requirement or the immediate research priority.

Edward Baker identified this distinction after reviewing the lattice and quaternionic constructions: “Specifically the simplification of using the 3d Laplacian was useful.” This note is the requested starting point for continuation. It supersedes the immediate lattice-construction priorities in [Note09][n09] and the next-step proposal in [Note12][n12], while preserving their identities and stated scopes. It consolidates established formulas and sets a research direction; it adds no new mathematical return to the seven already recorded under RTC-03.

## 1. The simplification to retain

Use the unchanged canonical definitions

\[
A(r)=\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-\pi n^2r^2},\qquad
\Theta(r)=1+2A(r),\qquad r=e^{2u},
\]
\[
H(t,z)=\int_0^\infty e^{tu^2}\Phi(u)\cos(zu)\,du,
\qquad \partial_tH=-\partial_z^2H.
\tag{1}
\]

Regard A and Theta as radial profiles on three-dimensional Euclidean space. Their arithmetic index remains n in Z. The standard radial Laplacian is

\[
\Delta_3 f=f''+\frac2r f'
=\frac1{r^2}\frac d{dr}\left(r^2f'\right).
\tag{2}
\]

For a single Gaussian,

\[
\Delta_d e^{-\pi n^2r^2}
=\left(4\pi^2n^4r^2-2d\pi n^2\right)e^{-\pi n^2r^2}.
\]

Thus dimension three supplies exactly the relative coefficients in the original source:

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\Phi(u)=\frac12r^{5/2}\Delta_3A(r)
       =\frac14r^{5/2}Q(r),\qquad Q=\Delta_3\Theta.}
\tag{3}
\]

This replaces an awkward polynomially weighted sum by a familiar differential operator acting on the elementary theta potential. It retains the original coefficients and introduces no shell multiplicities, parity characters, dyadic reconstruction or additional lattice sum. The factor r^(5/2) and logarithmic coordinate are still present and should remain visible when assessing further simplifications.

The equivalent earlier primitive identity is

\[
\psi(u)=e^uA(e^{2u}),\qquad
(\partial_u^2-1)\psi=4r^{5/2}\Delta_3A=8\Phi.
\tag{4}
\]

Equations (2)–(4) are established in [Note01, Section 2][n01] and the founding [Investigation04 Note20][prior20]. Start from these identities rather than attempting another higher-rank realization of A.

## 2. The exact observation and time dependence

Let

\[
Q_t(r)=e^{\frac t4\log^2r}Q(r).
\]

The complete original H is

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
H(t,z)=\frac18\int_1^\infty
r^{3/2}Q_t(r)\cos\!\left(\frac z2\log r\right)dr.}
\tag{5}
\]

This identity fixes the measure and normalization for subsequent work. The half-line u>=0 corresponds to the exterior r>=1; u=0 is the unit sphere, not the spatial origin. The full even continuation in u includes inversion-related radii below one.

The physical time law is

\[
\partial_tQ_t=\frac14\log^2r\,Q_t.
\tag{6}
\]

It is multiplication in the radial source variable. The appearance of Delta_3 in (3) does not turn Newman evolution into radial diffusion. Likewise, multiplying the potential by the time weight does not commute with its Laplacian:

\[
\Delta_3(wA)=w\Delta_3A+2w'A'+(\Delta_3w)A,
\qquad w=e^{t\log^2r/4}.
\tag{7}
\]

Any time-dependent potential must retain these terms or solve the correctly normalized Poisson problem below. The complete source tails justify the observation and parameter differentiation for all finite complex t,z; positivity statements here refer to real t.

## 3. Useful geometric structure already available

### Radial flux and Kelvin inversion

Theta modularity is ordinary three-dimensional Kelvin symmetry:

\[
\Theta(r)=r^{-1}\Theta(1/r),\qquad
Q(r)=r^{-5}Q(1/r),\qquad
Q_t(r)=r^{-5}Q_t(1/r).
\tag{8}
\]

For the static potential, define its radial flux factor F=r^2 Theta'. Then

\[
F'=r^2Q,\qquad F(0+)=-1,\qquad F(\infty)=0,
\qquad \int_0^\infty r^2Q(r)dr=1.
\tag{9}
\]

The actual flux through a sphere is 4 pi F. The source Q is positive for r>0, while the whole-space distributional equation includes the central charge:

\[
\Delta_{\mathbb R^3}\Theta=Q(|X|)-4\pi\delta_0.
\tag{10}
\]

At the inversion sphere, Theta'(1)=-Theta(1)/2. These boundary and contact terms are part of the simplification: the Laplacian makes them explicit. They cannot be omitted in a Green or divergence identity.

### The correctly normalized evolved potential

[Note01, Section 4][n01] already gives

\[
M_t=\int_0^\infty s^2Q_t(s)ds=16H(t,i),
\]
\[
\mathcal T_t(r)=M_t+
\int_r^\infty\left(\frac{s^2}{r}-s\right)Q_t(s)ds,
\qquad \mathcal T_0=\Theta.
\tag{11}
\]

Consequently

\[
r^2\mathcal T_t'(r)=-\int_r^\infty s^2Q_t(s)ds,
\qquad \Delta_3\mathcal T_t=Q_t\quad(r>0),
\]
\[
\mathcal T_t(r)=r^{-1}\mathcal T_t(1/r),\qquad
\Delta_{\mathbb R^3}\mathcal T_t=Q_t-4\pi M_t\delta_0.
\tag{12}
\]

For real t, M_t>0. The constant at infinity and the central charge both evolve with M_t; they are not fixed at their t=0 value. The integral in (11) specifies the harmonic ambiguity and the rapid tail at infinity. Reuse this normalization rather than introducing a second inverse Laplacian with unspecified boundary data.

### The observation variable in the same radius

[Note07, Section 3][n07] retains r as the spatial radius and uses

\[
\Psi_z(r)=r^{-1/2}\cos\!\left(\frac z2\log r\right),
\qquad
-\Delta_3\Psi_z=\frac{1+z^2}{4r^2}\Psi_z.
\tag{13}
\]

The corresponding whole-space pairing is

\[
H(t,z)=\frac1{64\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}Q_t(|X|)\Psi_z(|X|)\,dX.
\tag{14}
\]

This gives z a precise role as a frequency in logarithmic radius. It is a source pairing, not a characteristic determinant: a zero of H does not automatically become an eigenvalue of a homogeneous operator. The different construction with Euclidean radius rho=|u| in Note07, Section 2, remains optional background and must not be confused with r=exp(2u).

## 4. The next bounded continuation

The immediate task is to review and develop the simplifications arising from Delta_3, keeping A and its square arithmetic fixed. A useful first pass is:

1. **Compare the existing radial descriptions.** Use A or Theta as potential, Q_t as source, and r^2 T_t' as flux. Identify which formulation makes the desired operation simpler: differentiation, inversion, a boundary condition, or the complete observation (5). Avoid rederiving the dictionary as if it were a new result.
2. **Choose one consequence of the standard operator.** The natural first candidates are a radial Green identity with the logarithmic mode (13), or a relation between the flux in (12) and the observation. Specify the quantity that should become easier to understand or control before adding a new unknown or transform.
3. **Compare the complete result with the existing formula.** Retain both endpoints or the inversion boundary, all time-dependent normalization, and the full source. State exactly what has been removed or explained. If the calculation only reproduces the old primitive reconstruction, record that comparison and stop that variant.

There is a known benchmark for the third step. The exterior Green calculation in Note01, Section 3, already yields, for

\[
J(t,z)=\int_0^\infty e^{tu^2}\psi(u)\cos(zu)du,
\]
\[
8H=\frac12+(2t-z^2-1)J+4tzJ_z-4t^2J_{zz}.
\tag{15}
\]

The constant 1/2 is a boundary contribution. A proposed integration-by-parts simplification should be compared with (15), including its derivative and endpoint costs.

The first return may be a genuinely clearer complete representation, a useful source/flux relation, or a precise explanation of why a specified radial manipulation adds no benefit. It need not already prove a collision estimate. If an estimate is proposed, identify its consumer and domain before starting numerics.

## 5. What to leave aside and what to carry forward

The lattice and quaternionic constructions in Notes06 and 08–12 remain comparison material. They established exact identities but have not demonstrated enough overall simplification to justify continuing to optimize their shell weights, dyadic rules or divisor inversions as the default next task. This is a priority decision, not an impossibility claim about higher-dimensional lattices.

The quaternion Dirac factorization D^2=-Delta_3 may be used if a first-order formulation removes an actual difficulty. It is not required for the radial program, and merely writing a quaternionic exponential is not itself a further simplification. No Fueter equation in Newman time is assumed.

Retain the previously proved limitations when returning to collision questions. The forced boundary equation in Note01, Sections 6–7, includes a forcing term in its Wronskian identity; positive source and positive response alone do not prevent cancellation. The [collision controls][controls] keep their original scopes. Neither a new coordinate expression nor a standard positive operator supplies a collision theorem by itself.

The [result index][results], particularly [theta arithmetic][arithmetic] and [geometric realizations][geometry], and the [avoid index][avoid] apply. The most relevant cautions are [coordinate lifts][a03], [omitted coupled terms][a12], [normalization slips][a08] and [scoped conclusions][a07]. Under [the target classification][a01], this note is a continuation brief built on established representations. It proposes no new sign criterion, performs no new numerical experiment, and changes no certified region or Newman bound.
